arguments.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs.
arguments.who_benefits: Boat owners seeking superior protection and reduced upkeep; Jotun benefits by commanding premium prices and building brand equity in the consumer segment.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If owners view marine coatings as a necessary investment that prevents fouling and saves time/money, they will be willing to pay more for a product that delivers those benefits.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can capture value by pricing coatings above generic marine paints, leveraging its reputation for performance, and potentially bundling with services or accessories.
assumptions: Boat owners are willing to allocate a portion of their maintenance budget to premium coatings.
Performance claims (e.g., reduced fouling, longer lifespan) are credible and measurable.
Jotun can communicate these benefits effectively to DIY and professional users.
predictions: In a test offering a premium marine coating at a 20% price premium versus a generic alternative, at least 30% of surveyed residential boat owners will indicate intent to purchase.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with perceived biofouling reduction and cost savings over a 2‑year period.

arguments.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive personalized recommendations from marine professionals (e.g., yacht captains, marina staff) who trust Jotun’s performance and recommend it for their own boats.
arguments.who_benefits: Boat owners gain confidence in the product through trusted third-party endorsement; Jotun benefits by leveraging professional credibility to drive sales and build brand trust in the consumer segment.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If owners perceive marine professionals as reliable sources of product advice, they will be more likely to purchase Jotun coatings, even if the price is similar to competitors, because they trust the recommendation.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can capture value by offering premium pricing justified by expert endorsement, and potentially bundling with professional services or training.
assumptions: Marine professionals have sufficient experience to identify performance benefits of Jotun coatings.
Owners trust professionals’ recommendations more than marketing claims.
Jotun can reach and engage these professionals through partnerships or marketing.
predictions: In a test where residential boat owners are shown a recommendation letter from a marina captain endorsing Jotun coatings, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a control group shown generic information.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with the perceived credibility of the recommending professional.

arguments.quote: Moreover, 14 % of the boat owners admitted to have used paints that are not allowed in the area studied and this is a problem well-known from other studies too (Swedish Transport Agency 2010 ).
arguments.does_not_show: The source does not show that residential boat owners are willing to pay a premium for marine coatings that reduce biofouling, nor that they perceive such benefits as credible.

arguments.quote: Jotun Decorative supplies coatings for commercial buildings, public buildings, and homes, and serves both the professional and DIY customer directly and through a network of Jotun Multicolor Centers.
arguments.does_not_show: The source does not provide evidence that marine professionals recommend Jotun coatings, nor that owners trust those recommendations. It only confirms Jotun serves DIY customers and professionals.

arguments.name: Premium vs Professional Recommendation Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are residential boat owners recruited via marine forums and social media. They are shown one of two product descriptions: (A) a premium marine coating highlighting biofouling reduction and performance claims, priced 20% above a generic alternative; (B) the same premium description plus a letter from a marina captain stating "I recommend Jotun because it consistently outperforms competitors and reduces biofouling." Participants indicate purchase intent on a 0‑100
arguments.sample: 300 residential boat owners (150 per condition). Recruitment cost €1,500; survey platform €500; incentives €500. Total €2,500.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (0‑100). Secondary: willingness to pay premium (percentage above generic price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium description will be at least 30% higher than for the generic description, even without the professional recommendation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the premium description will be at least 15% higher when accompanied by the marina captain’s recommendation letter, compared to the premium description alone.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the premium description alone is at least 30% higher than the generic description, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition (support T1). If the premium description with the captain’s letter is at least 15% higher than the premium

tool_result.brief: Jotun is a Norwegian maker of marine, protective and powder coatings for shipyards, ship owners, infrastructure and industry. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Many sources were written after the decision date: reason only from what was knowable on that date, and do not use what you may know about later events. Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify Jotun investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on publicly available information known by mid-2024.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify what Jotun already sells to individual buyers (if any).
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive positioning, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential boat owners, DIY home protection).
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering existing coatings directly to individual buyers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B marine, protective, and industrial coatings.
4) Partner with or license the technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Jotun’s own consumer brand.
5) Target a different customer segment, such as automotive or construction, using the same marine coating technology.

T1.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs.
T1.who_benefits: Boat owners seeking superior protection and reduced upkeep; Jotun benefits by commanding premium prices and building brand equity in the consumer segment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If owners view marine coatings as a necessary investment that prevents fouling and saves time/money, they will be willing to pay more for a product that delivers those benefits.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can capture value by pricing coatings above generic marine paints, leveraging its reputation for performance, and potentially bundling with services or accessories.
assumptions: Boat owners are willing to allocate a portion of their maintenance budget to premium coatings.
Performance claims (e.g., reduced fouling, longer lifespan) are credible and measurable.
Jotun can communicate these benefits effectively to DIY and professional users.
predictions: In a test offering a premium marine coating at a 20% price premium versus a generic alternative, at least 30% of surveyed residential boat owners will indicate intent to purchase.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with perceived biofouling reduction and cost savings over a 2‑year period.
T1.first_claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs.

T2.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive personalized recommendations from marine professionals (e.g., yacht captains, marina staff) who trust Jotun’s performance and recommend it for their own boats.
T2.who_benefits: Boat owners gain confidence in the product through trusted third-party endorsement; Jotun benefits by leveraging professional credibility to drive sales and build brand trust in the consumer segment.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If owners perceive marine professionals as reliable sources of product advice, they will be more likely to purchase Jotun coatings, even if the price is similar to competitors, because they trust the recommendation.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can capture value by offering premium pricing justified by expert endorsement, and potentially bundling with professional services or training.
assumptions: Marine professionals have sufficient experience to identify performance benefits of Jotun coatings.
Owners trust professionals’ recommendations more than marketing claims.
Jotun can reach and engage these professionals through partnerships or marketing.
predictions: In a test where residential boat owners are shown a recommendation letter from a marina captain endorsing Jotun coatings, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a control group shown generic information.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with the perceived credibility of the recommending professional.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify Jotun investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on publicly available information known by mid-2024.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify what Jotun already sells to individual buyers (if any).
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive positioning, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential boat owners, DIY home protection).
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering existing coatings directly to individual buyers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B marine, protective, and industrial coatings.
4) Partner with or license the technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Jotun’s own consumer brand.
5) Target a different customer segment, such as automotive or construction, using the same marine coating technology.

T1.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs.
T1.who_benefits: Boat owners seeking superior protection and reduced upkeep; Jotun benefits by commanding premium prices and building brand equity in the consumer segment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If owners view marine coatings as a necessary investment that prevents fouling and saves time/money, they will be willing to pay more for a product that delivers those benefits.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can capture value by pricing coatings above generic marine paints, leveraging its reputation for performance, and potentially bundling with services or accessories.
assumptions: Boat owners are willing to allocate a portion of their maintenance budget to premium coatings.
Performance claims (e.g., reduced fouling, longer lifespan) are credible and measurable.
Jotun can communicate these benefits effectively to DIY and professional users.
predictions: In a test offering a premium marine coating at a 20% price premium versus a generic alternative, at least 30% of surveyed residential boat owners will indicate intent to purchase.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with perceived biofouling reduction and cost savings over a 2‑year period.
T1.first_claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs.

T2.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive personalized recommendations from marine professionals (e.g., yacht captains, marina staff) who trust Jotun’s performance and recommend it for their own boats.
T2.who_benefits: Boat owners gain confidence in the product through trusted third-party endorsement; Jotun benefits by leveraging professional credibility to drive sales and build brand trust in the consumer segment.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If owners perceive marine professionals as reliable sources of product advice, they will be more likely to purchase Jotun coatings, even if the price is similar to competitors, because they trust the recommendation.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can capture value by offering premium pricing justified by expert endorsement, and potentially bundling with professional services or training.
assumptions: Marine professionals have sufficient experience to identify performance benefits of Jotun coatings.
Owners trust professionals’ recommendations more than marketing claims.
Jotun can reach and engage these professionals through partnerships or marketing.
predictions: In a test where residential boat owners are shown a recommendation letter from a marina captain endorsing Jotun coatings, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a control group shown generic information.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with the perceived credibility of the recommending professional.
T2.first_claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive personalized recommendations from marine professionals (e.g., yacht captains, marina staff) who trust Jotun’s performance and recommend it for their own boats.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B proposition (clinics, health clubs) by offering the analyser as a rental or subscription service to increase market penetration.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial and institutional customers, maintaining the current product and distribution model.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home appliances or wearable devices.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells devices at a premium price directly to consumers, retaining margin and brand equity.
assumptions: Consumers trust Tanita’s medical-grade technology.
There is a sizable segment of consumers willing to pay for home body-fat monitoring.
Regulatory environment allows home use of bioelectrical impedance devices.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser at a price above $100.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating alternatives.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before 1993; later developments are not usable.
Financial data for Tanita is not available in the dossier; any financial conclusions must be noted as unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B proposition (clinics, health clubs) by offering the analyser as a rental or subscription service to increase market penetration.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial and institutional customers, maintaining the current product and distribution model.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home appliances or wearable devices.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells devices at a premium price directly to consumers, retaining margin and brand equity.
assumptions: Consumers trust Tanita’s medical-grade technology.
There is a sizable segment of consumers willing to pay for home body-fat monitoring.
Regulatory environment allows home use of bioelectrical impedance devices.

position.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test whether health-conscious consumers will purchase a home body-fat analyser at $120 and whether status-conscious consumers will purchase at $180. The test will resolve whether T1 (health-driven demand) or T2 (status-driven demand) is more likely. frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating alternatives.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before 1993; later developments are not usable.
Financial data for Tanita is not available in the dossier; any financial conclusions must be noted as unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B proposition (clinics, health clubs) by offering the analyser as a rental or subscription service to increase market penetration.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial and institutional customers, maintaining the current product and distribution model.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home appliances or wearable devices.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyzer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 500 respondents (250 health-conscious, 250 status-conscious) from regions with high obesity rates. Randomly assign participants to one of two price points: $120 (health-focused) or $180 (status-focused). Ask: "Would you purchase this device for home use?" (Yes/No). Also ask willingness-to-pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. Collect demographic and self-reported health/lifestyle data.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and WTP (7-point scale). Secondary: repeat purchase intent after 3 months (optional).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $120 than status-conscious segment.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $180 than health-conscious segment.

X1.decision_rule: If health-conscious segment purchase intent at $120 exceeds status-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for health segment is at least $120, then T1 is supported. If status-conscious segment purchase intent at $180 exceeds health-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for status segment is at least $180, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, pricing, or willingness to pay for a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Maintain the current B2B focus and continue monitoring consumer demand through surveys or pilot tests before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers seeking accurate personal body-fat monitoring; also potentially status-conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for a visible health signal.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced home body-fat analyser leveraging Tanita’s medical-grade bioelectrical impedance technology, sold directly to consumers at $120‑$180, offering precise health data and brand prestige.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test purchase intent and willingness to pay at different price points. If the health segment shows higher intent at $120 and meets the 10‑point threshold, proceed to develop a consumer
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (health-driven demand) and T2 (status-driven demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand evidence from 1993. The survey will resolve which mechanism is more likely.
would_change_if: If the survey shows status-conscious consumers at $180 achieve a 10‑point advantage over health-conscious consumers, we would shift focus to a status-driven proposition.
If neither segment meets the 10‑point threshold, we would abandon consumer expansion and remain focused on B2B markets.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyzer
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 500 respondents (250 health-conscious, 250 status-conscious) from regions with high obesity rates. Randomly assign participants to one of two price points: $120 (health-focused) or $180 (status-focused). Ask: "Would you purchase this device for home use?" (Yes/No). Also ask willingness-to-pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. Collect demographic and self-reported health/lifestyle data.
arguments.sample: 500 respondents (250 per segment)
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and WTP (7-point scale). Secondary: repeat purchase intent after 3 months (optional).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $120 than status-conscious segment.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $180 than health-conscious segment.

arguments.decision_rule: If health-conscious segment purchase intent at $120 exceeds status-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for health segment is at least $120, then T1 is supported. If status-conscious segment purchase intent at $180 exceeds health-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for status segment is at least $180, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test whether health-conscious consumers will purchase a home body-fat analyser at $120 and whether status-conscious consumers will purchase at $180. The test will resolve whether T1 (health-driven demand) or T2 (status-driven demand) is more likely. Until the test results are available, maintain the current B2B focus and do not invest in a consumer proposition.

arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 (health-driven demand) and T2 (status-driven demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand evidence from 1993. The survey will resolve which mechanism is more likely.

If neither segment meets the 10‑point threshold, we would abandon consumer expansion and remain focused on B2B markets.

position.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test whether health-conscious consumers will purchase a home body-fat analyser at $120 and whether status-conscious consumers will purchase at $180. The test will resolve whether T1 (health-driven demand) or T2 (status-driven demand) is more likely. Until the test results are available, maintain the current B2B focus and do not invest in a consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating alternatives.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before 1993; later developments are not usable.
Financial data for Tanita is not available in the dossier; any financial conclusions must be noted as unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B proposition (clinics, health clubs) by offering the analyser as a rental or subscription service to increase market penetration.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial and institutional customers, maintaining the current product and distribution model.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home appliances or wearable devices.

T1.claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a reliable tool for personal health monitoring, and Tanita can capture value by selling premium-priced devices directly to consumers.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking accurate health data; Tanita gains higher margins through direct sales.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of body composition as a health indicator (e.g., heart disease, diabetes) makes consumers willing to purchase devices that provide precise measurements.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells devices at a premium price directly to consumers, retaining margin and brand equity.
assumptions: Consumers trust Tanita’s medical-grade technology.
There is a sizable segment of consumers willing to pay for home body-fat monitoring.
Regulatory environment allows home use of bioelectrical impedance devices.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser at a price above $100.
Sales of a consumer version will be driven by regions with higher obesity rates and stronger health awareness.
Repeat purchase rate for replacement sensors or additional services will be above 20%.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells devices at a premium price through retail channels, leveraging brand equity and design appeal to capture consumer spending.
assumptions: Consumers associate Tanita with precision and quality from its professional market presence.
There is a segment of consumers willing to pay for a health device that signals status.
Retail distribution channels will stock a consumer version.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser at a price above $150, driven by design and brand.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with higher disposable incomes and strong consumer health trends.
Repeat purchase will be driven by accessory purchases (extra sensors, decorative covers) rather than core device.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyzer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 500 respondents (250 health-conscious, 250 status-conscious) from regions with high obesity rates. Randomly assign participants to one of two price points: $120 (health-focused) or $180 (status-focused). Ask: "Would you purchase this device for home use?" (Yes/No). Also ask willingness-to-pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. Collect demographic and self-reported health/lifestyle data.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and WTP (7-point scale). Secondary: repeat purchase intent after 3 months (optional).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $120 than status-conscious segment.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $180 than health-conscious segment.

X1.decision_rule: If health-conscious segment purchase intent at $120 exceeds status-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for health segment is at least $120, then T1 is supported. If status-conscious segment purchase intent at $180 exceeds health-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for status segment is at least $180, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, pricing, or willingness to pay for a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Maintain the current B2B focus and continue monitoring consumer demand through surveys or pilot tests before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers seeking accurate personal body-fat monitoring; also potentially status-conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for a visible health signal.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced home body-fat analyser leveraging Tanita’s medical-grade bioelectrical impedance technology, sold directly to consumers at $120‑$180, offering precise health data and brand prestige.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test purchase intent and willingness to pay at different price points. If the health segment shows higher intent at $120 and meets the 10‑point threshold, proceed to develop a consumer
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (health-driven demand) and T2 (status-driven demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand evidence from 1993. The survey will resolve which mechanism is more likely.
would_change_if: If the survey shows status-conscious consumers at $180 achieve a 10‑point advantage over health-conscious consumers, we would shift focus to a status-driven proposition.
If neither segment meets the 10‑point threshold, we would abandon consumer expansion and remain focused on B2B markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating alternatives.

Financial data for Tanita is not available in the dossier; any financial conclusions must be noted as unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).

3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial and institutional customers, maintaining the current product and distribution model.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home appliances or wearable devices.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyzer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 500 respondents (250 health-conscious, 250 status-conscious) from regions with high obesity rates. Randomly assign participants to one of two price points: $120 (health-focused) or $180 (status-focused). Ask: "Would you purchase this device for home use?" (Yes/No). Also ask willingness-to-pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. Collect demographic and self-reported health/lifestyle data.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and WTP (7-point scale). Secondary: repeat purchase intent after 3 months (optional).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $120 than status-conscious segment.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $180 than health-conscious segment.

X1.decision_rule: If health-conscious segment purchase intent at $120 exceeds status-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for health segment is at least $120, then T1 is supported. If status-conscious segment purchase intent at $180 exceeds health-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for status segment is at least $180, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, pricing, or willingness to pay for a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Maintain the current B2B focus and continue monitoring consumer demand through surveys or pilot tests before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers seeking accurate personal body-fat monitoring; also potentially status-conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for a visible health signal.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced home body-fat analyser leveraging Tanita’s medical-grade bioelectrical impedance technology, sold directly to consumers at $120‑$180, offering precise health data and brand prestige.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test purchase intent and willingness to pay at different price points. If the health segment shows higher intent at $120 and meets the 10‑point threshold, proceed to develop a consumer
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (health-driven demand) and T2 (status-driven demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand evidence from 1993. The survey will resolve which mechanism is more likely.
would_change_if: If the survey shows status-conscious consumers at $180 achieve a 10‑point advantage over health-conscious consumers, we would shift focus to a status-driven proposition.
If neither segment meets the 10‑point threshold, we would abandon consumer expansion and remain focused on B2B markets.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyzer
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 500 respondents (250 health-conscious, 250 status-conscious) from regions with high obesity rates. Randomly assign participants to one of two price points: $120 (health-focused) or $180 (status-focused). Ask: "Would you purchase this device for home use?" (Yes/No). Also ask willingness-to-pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. Collect demographic and self-reported health/lifestyle data.
arguments.sample: 500 respondents (250 per segment)
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and WTP (7-point scale). Secondary: repeat purchase intent after 3 months (optional).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $120 than status-conscious segment.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status-conscious segment will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP at $180 than health-conscious segment.

arguments.decision_rule: If health-conscious segment purchase intent at $120 exceeds status-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for health segment is at least $120, then T1 is supported. If status-conscious segment purchase intent at $180 exceeds health-conscious segment by at least 10 percentage points AND average WTP for status segment is at least $180, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test whether health-conscious consumers will purchase a home body-fat analyser at $120 and whether status-conscious consumers will purchase at $180. The test will resolve whether T1 (health-driven demand) or T2 (status-driven demand) is more likely. Until the test results are available, maintain the current B2B focus and do not invest in a consumer proposition.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, pricing, or willingness to pay for a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a reliable tool for personal health monitoring, and Tanita can capture value by selling premium-priced devices directly to consumers.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Maintain the current B2B focus and continue monitoring consumer demand through surveys or pilot tests before committing resources.
arguments.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers seeking accurate personal body-fat monitoring; also potentially status-conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for a visible health signal.
arguments.value_proposition: A premium-priced home body-fat analyser leveraging Tanita’s medical-grade bioelectrical impedance technology, sold directly to consumers at $120‑$180, offering precise health data and brand prestige.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test purchase intent and willingness to pay at different price points. If the health segment shows higher intent at $120 and meets the 10‑point threshold, proceed to develop a consumer
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 (health-driven demand) and T2 (status-driven demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand evidence from 1993. The survey will resolve which mechanism is more likely.
would_change_if: If the survey shows status-conscious consumers at $180 achieve a 10‑point advantage over health-conscious consumers, we would shift focus to a status-driven proposition.
If neither segment meets the 10‑point threshold, we would abandon consumer expansion and remain focused on B2B markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available by late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) and not just general consumer interest.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without creating a consumer proposition (status quo).
3) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications rather than building a proprietary consumer product.
4) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current markets (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).

Consumers are willing to invest in safety equipment that provides a clear survival advantage.
The 406 MHz frequency is reliable for distress alerts in remote areas.
predictions: If a survey of outdoor recreation participants shows >30% would purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon within 12 months, demand justifies production.

constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed 10‑week, €15,000 consumer preference survey (Test X1) to measure purchase intent for outdoor recreation versus emergency preparedness before any product development or marketing commitment.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available by late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) and not just general consumer interest.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without creating a consumer proposition (status quo).
3) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications rather than building a proprietary consumer product.
4) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current markets (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).

They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A describes a 406 MHz distress beacon marketed for outdoor recreation (hiking, camping, mountaineering) with a price of $300-500 and a
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = Very unlikely, 7 = Very likely) and willingness to pay (EUR equivalent). Secondary measure: self-reported likelihood to recommend to a friend.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the outdoor recreation condition (difference of at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the emergency preparedness condition (difference of at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale).

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between the two conditions is at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting the condition with the higher intent. If the difference is less than 1.5 points,

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, purchase intent, or adoption for outdoor recreation. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed 10‑week, €15,000 consumer preference survey (Test X1) to measure purchase intent for outdoor recreation versus emergency preparedness before any product development or marketing commitment.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, campers, mountaineers) and search‑and‑rescue agencies that can locate and respond to distress signals.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreation users, leveraging the 406 MHz distress beacon to provide reliable emergency alert in remote areas where other communication methods are limited.
final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week timeline and budget of €15,000.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (outdoor recreation) and T2 (emergency preparedness) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of consumer demand or purchase intent for the 406 MHz beacon.
would_change_if: If the survey shows a purchase intent difference of at least 1.5 points on the 7‑point scale in favor of outdoor recreation, we would proceed to develop a consumer proposition for that segment.
If the survey shows a similar or lower difference, we would reconsider the investment and explore other options, such as licensing the technology or expanding the B2B focus.

result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. In this simulated warehouse test, a new label printer reduced packing errors slightly. Nothing about wearers or buyers was measured.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, purchase intent, or adoption for outdoor recreation. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency alert in remote areas where other communication methods are limited.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed 10‑week, €15,000 consumer preference survey (Test X1) to measure purchase intent for outdoor recreation versus emergency preparedness before any product development or marketing commitment.
arguments.target_customer: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, campers, mountaineers) and search‑and‑rescue agencies that can locate and respond to distress signals.
arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreation users, leveraging the 406 MHz distress beacon to provide reliable emergency alert in remote areas where other communication methods are limited.
arguments.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week timeline and budget of €15,000.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 (outdoor recreation) and T2 (emergency preparedness) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of consumer demand or purchase intent for the 406 MHz beacon.
would_change_if: If the survey shows a purchase intent difference of at least 1.5 points on the 7‑point scale in favor of outdoor recreation, we would proceed to develop a consumer proposition for that segment.
If the survey shows a similar or lower difference, we would reconsider the investment and explore other options, such as licensing the technology or expanding the B2B focus.

tool_result.question: It is late 2002. Should ACR Electronics develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology? What evidence would justify that investment?
tool_result.brief: ACR Electronics is a Fort Lauderdale maker of emergency radio beacons for ships and aircraft and of survival lights for military and commercial marine users. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Many sources were written after the decision date: reason only from what was knowable on that date, and do not use what you may know about later events. Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available by late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) and not just general consumer interest.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without creating a consumer proposition (status quo).
3) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications rather than building a proprietary consumer product.
4) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current markets (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency alert in remote areas where other communication methods fail.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers engaged in high‑risk outdoor activities (e.g., hikers, climbers, remote boaters) who need a distress alert system that works without cellular or radio signals.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently rely on cellular phones or radio for emergency communication but face limited coverage in remote locations. A 406 MHz beacon offers a proven, satellite‑based distress alert that can be deployed without infrastructure.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online, capturing premium pricing for a specialized safety product.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation is growing in 2002 and will continue to increase.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety devices that work in remote environments.
The 406 MHz frequency is reliable for distress alerts in those environments.
predictions: If a test offers a limited number of beacons to outdoor recreation groups, adoption rates will be higher than for other consumer segments.
Surveyed users will cite remote coverage as the primary reason for purchase.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with significant outdoor recreation activity.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Maintain the current B2B/industrial focus and conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and actual purchase between outdoor recreation and emergency preparedness groups. The test will resolve whether T1 (outdoor recreation demand) or T2 (emergency preparedness demand) is better supported by evidence.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, climbers, remote boaters) and emergency preparedness consumers (coastal residents, high‑risk areas) who need reliable distress alerts in remote or high‑risk environments.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that provides proven, satellite‑based distress alerting in remote locations, meeting regulatory compliance and offering a safety solution for consumers who currently rely on cellular or radio signals.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeframe and €20,000 budget, measuring purchase intent and actual purchase. Use the decision rule to determine which segment shows stronger demand.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer purchase behavior for 406 MHz beacons in 2002. The test is needed to differentiate between outdoor recreation and emergency preparedness demand.
would_change_if: If the test shows outdoor recreation purchase intent and actual purchase significantly exceed emergency preparedness, T1 would be favored and investment could proceed.
If the test shows emergency preparedness purchase intent and actual purchase significantly exceed outdoor recreation, T2 would be favored and a different consumer proposition would be considered.
If the test shows no significant difference or low overall demand, the recommendation would be to remain focused on B2B/industrial markets.

X1.name: Survey-based willingness-to-pay test for convenience vs status motivations
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a description of a 1962 John Deere lawn and garden tractor (highlighting either convenience features or status/prestige messaging). They are asked: "How much would you pay for this tractor today?" (open numeric response). A separate follow-up question probes primary motivation (convenience vs status).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 30-65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for region and homeownership status.
X1.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for the convenience-framed tractor versus the status-framed tractor. Secondary measure: proportion of participants selecting "convenience" as primary motivation for each frame.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and higher proportion citing convenience for the convenience frame.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and higher proportion citing status for the status frame.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed survey-based willingness-to-pay test to empirically compare homeowner motivations for convenience versus status. Until the test results are available, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition; instead, maintain the existing dealer model and monitor market signals.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with yards in the United States who are considering purchasing a lawn and garden tractor for yard work.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions the tractor as a convenient, time-saving tool for yard work, leveraging Deere’s existing tractor engineering and dealer network.
final.next_action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey with 500 homeowners, analyze results against the decision rule, and decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer offering or maintain the current model.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources published before 1962; no direct consumer demand data or sales figures exist. The motivations of homeowners in 1962 are uncertain, and the test is needed to resolve this.

If the survey confirms a 15%+ willingness-to-pay advantage for the time-savings description, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on productivity and time efficiency. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market opportunity for a new consumer product.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing distribution network of independent dealers and its current product portfolio (farm tractors, combines, industrial equipment).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale gardening, hobby farming, or a niche agricultural activity) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without a differentiated proposition (e.g., mass‑market small tractors or consumer‑grade equipment) leveraging the existing dealer network.
3) No expansion – continue focusing on the current B2B and existing dealer model, maintaining the current product and market scope.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Status vs Time-Savings Motivations
X1.method: Online survey with hypothetical purchase scenario. Participants view a description of a 1962 John Deere lawn and garden tractor (highlighting either prestige/status or time-saving features). They are asked: (1) "What is the maximum price you would pay for this tractor?" (2) "How likely are you to purchase it?" (3) "Which motivation (status or time savings) best describes why you would buy it?" Participants are randomly assigned to see either the status or time-saving description. The survey is run via a panel of 500 U.S. homeowners, recruited to represent the 1962 demographic.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners, recruited via an online panel, matched for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect 1962 demographic distribution.
X1.measure: 1) Maximum price willingness-to-pay (EUR). 2) Purchase intent (1‑0 scale). 3) Motivation selection (status vs time savings).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market opportunity for a new consumer product.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing distribution network of independent dealers and its current product portfolio (farm tractors, combines, industrial equipment).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale gardening, hobby farming, or a niche agricultural activity) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without a differentiated proposition (e.g., mass‑market small tractors or consumer‑grade equipment) leveraging the existing dealer network.
3) No expansion – continue focusing on the current B2B and existing dealer model, maintaining the current product and market scope.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market opportunity for a new consumer product.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing distribution network of independent dealers and its current product portfolio (farm tractors, combines, industrial equipment).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale gardening, hobby farming, or a niche agricultural activity) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without a differentiated proposition (e.g., mass‑market small tractors or consumer‑grade equipment) leveraging the existing dealer network.
3) No expansion – continue focusing on the current B2B and existing dealer model, maintaining the current product and market scope.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Status vs Time-Savings Motivations
X1.method: Online survey with hypothetical purchase scenario. Participants view a description of a 1962 John Deere lawn and garden tractor (highlighting either prestige/status or time-saving features). They are asked: (1) "What is the maximum price you would pay for this tractor?" (2) "How likely are you to purchase it?" (3) "Which motivation (status or time savings) best describes why you would buy it?" Participants are randomly assigned to see either the status or time-saving description. The survey is run via a panel of 500 U.S. homeowners, recruited to represent the 1962 demographic.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners, recruited via an online panel, matched for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect 1962 demographic distribution.
X1.measure: 1) Maximum price willingness-to-pay (EUR). 2) Purchase intent (1‑0 scale). 3) Motivation selection (status vs time savings).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market opportunity for a new consumer product.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing distribution network of independent dealers and its current product portfolio (farm tractors, combines, industrial equipment).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale gardening, hobby farming, or a niche agricultural activity) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without a differentiated proposition (e.g., mass‑market small tractors or consumer‑grade equipment) leveraging the existing dealer network.
3) No expansion – continue focusing on the current B2B and existing dealer model, maintaining the current product and market scope.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Status vs Time-Savings Motivations
X1.method: Online survey with hypothetical purchase scenario. Participants view a description of a 1962 John Deere lawn and garden tractor (highlighting either prestige/status or time-saving features). They are asked: (1) "What is the maximum price you would pay for this tractor?" (2) "How likely are you to purchase it?" (3) "Which motivation (status or time savings) best describes why you would buy it?" Participants are randomly assigned to see either the status or time-saving description. The survey is run via a panel of 500 U.S. homeowners, recruited to represent the 1962 demographic.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners, recruited via an online panel, matched for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect 1962 demographic distribution.
X1.measure: 1) Maximum price willingness-to-pay (EUR). 2) Purchase intent (1‑0 scale). 3) Motivation selection (status vs time savings).
